---
title: "Working in Codespaces"
---

A GitHub Codespace is a remote Linux computer that you control through a
browser-based Visual Studio Code interface. The interface contains many tools,
but only a small subset is needed for this course.

## The four areas you will use

**Explorer**  
The file icon in the left activity bar. Use it to open notebooks and files and
to navigate between `course/` and `work/`.

**Notebook editor**  
Opening an `.ipynb` file displays a Jupyter notebook. Run cells with the
triangular **Run** button or with `Shift+Enter`. If you are asked to select a
kernel, choose the Python environment provided by the Codespace.

**Terminal**  
Open it with **Terminal → New Terminal**. Course commands such as
`update-course` and `start-lab` are run here.

**Source Control**  
The branch-shaped icon in the left activity bar. Use it to commit your work and
synchronize it with GitHub.

## Reopening your existing Codespace

After the first session, do **not** create a new Codespace every time.

You can reopen the existing one from either:

- your personal workspace repository → **Code → Codespaces**; or
- <https://github.com/codespaces>.

Starting an existing stopped Codespace is normally much faster than creating a
new one.

## Where to work

The workspace follows a simple rule:

```text
course/   instructor-controlled material
work/     your personal work
```

Your notebooks and answers belong under directories such as:

```text
work/lab01/
work/lab02/
```

Do not use `course/` as a working directory. New or corrected course material
may replace files there.

## Uploading a local file

Some laboratories may ask you to upload a CIF file or a CRYSTAL output from
your own computer.

Navigate to the appropriate directory under `work/` in the Explorer and drag
the local file into the Explorer. Check that the file appears in the intended
directory before continuing.

## Downloading a file

To copy a result from the Codespace to your computer, right-click the file in
the Explorer and select **Download**.

## A few useful terminal commands

You only need a very small amount of Linux for the notebook part of the course:

```bash
pwd
```

shows the current directory.

```bash
ls
```

lists files and directories.

```bash
cd work/lab01
```

moves into a directory.

```bash
cd ..
```

moves one level upward.

These are simply tools used to inspect and analyse mineral-science data.

Continue with **[Save, sync and stop](04-save-sync-stop.qmd)**.
